P2: the resume bar is now claimable completely, not two-thirds. P4 closed the epoch gap.

P4 added a real end-to-end test (packages/server/test/pty-ws.test.ts, test-only, their
lane) that does exactly what you asked for: host.spawn() called twice on the same
sessionId (the actual destructive replace), observed over the real frame codec with no
mocking of PtyHostService or pty-ws-server. Result, their words, matches what the byte-
handling law requires:
  - old socket gets a CLOSE frame, provably never an {type:'exit'} TEXT frame (checked the
    socket's entire frame history, not just the last message)
  - reconnecting gets attached.epoch !== the original epoch — a genuinely different value,
    read off the wire, not inferred
  - hasReplay:true, and the new stream's replay/live body contains the NEW process's output
    and does NOT contain the OLD process's output — no bleed-through across the replace

Combining that with what was already proven on my side: ptyTransport.test.ts:125 ("RESETS
when the epoch changes (a respawn), even without a byte rewind") unit-tests the CLIENT
reaction to exactly this frame shape — real product code (_handleAttached's epoch-equality
compare), a simulated frame sequence standing in for the server. P4's test proves the real
server actually produces that frame shape; mine proves the real client correctly reacts to
it. Together that's the full path, not an assumption bridging the two halves.

All three resume-bar claims now have real (not simulated-on-both-ends) evidence:
  - offset resume + replay: confirmed earlier (my fresh-tab reloads + P4's raw-socket probe)
  - epoch / authoritative reset on respawn: confirmed just now (P4's new test + my existing
    unit coverage, composed)

Nothing broken, nothing outstanding on this job from my side.
